data.title: Which ETFs Give You Alphabet After The Air Force Cloud Breach?
data.description:
You might like Alphabet for its search, video and cloud businesses, but owning the stock alone means carrying Alphabet specific risks by yourself. Simply Wall St flags that further fines, product limits or forced changes to how it runs search and ads could cut into advertising reach and money made from artificial intelligence. Holding Alphabet inside a fund that spreads your money across many holdings changes how much those single company risks can move your overall portfolio, and also limits how much upside Alphabet can drive on its own.

Right now the headline is security. Hackers breached the US Air Force Cloud One system that runs on infrastructure from Alphabet and other tech giants, disrupting upgrades and touching sensitive data. That kind of event affects how customers think about cloud reliability and how they choose providers. If you still want Alphabet in that mix, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) such as IWF, VUG and IVW give you a way to own it as part of a wider portfolio rather than on its own.

Picking stocks directly instead? Compare Alphabet with 52 AI infrastructure stocks.

iShares Russell 1000 Growth ETF (IWF)

IWF tilts heavily toward US growth sectors, with large slices in semiconductors, interactive media, hardware and software. Alphabet is a meaningful part of that mix at 9.96% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 in IWF puts about US$100 into Alphabet. A large share of the remaining exposure runs through other sizeable tech and growth stocks such as NVIDIA and Apple, which together make up 21.1% of the fund and shape much of its tech-heavy profile.

Alphabet’s high level of non-cash earnings can make its reported profits harder to interpret, because items such as accruals and stock-based pay can blur the relationship between earnings and cash. IWF addresses that company-specific characteristic primarily by pairing Alphabet with businesses whose profits depend on different products and customers, for example NVIDIA’s chip demand and Apple’s hardware and services. The fund still concentrates meaningfully in large US growth franchises whose cash flows are used to support their current valuations.

Not every stock inside IWF is priced the same way. Find out how many of IWF's holdings look undervalued.

Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (VUG)

Apple and NVIDIA dominate VUG’s roster, together covering 26.5% of the ETF and pulling a lot of your exposure toward semiconductors and hardware. The broader mix looks a lot like IWF, with large slices in semiconductors, technology hardware, systems software and interactive media. Alphabet sits behind those giants as the #4 position at 7.97% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 in VUG quietly puts about US$80 into Alphabet while the rest spreads across 141 holdings.

Alphabet still faces the risk that extra fines, tighter rules or changes to how it runs search and ads could limit advertising reach and AI related income. VUG will not cancel that. However, its stakes in areas such as pharmaceuticals, automobile manufacturers and transaction and payment processing services mean more of your money relies on different industries than Alphabet alone offers.

iShares S&P 500 Growth ETF (IVW)

IVW gives Alphabet a real slice at 9.08% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 puts about US$91 into the stock. The rest of the money tracks a growth-heavy mix that closely resembles VUG, with 21.8% in semiconductors, 13.1% in systems software and 8.2% in technology hardware, storage and peripherals. NVIDIA and Microsoft together take 22.8% of IVW, while pharmaceuticals, broadline retail and multi sector holdings add exposure to different drivers than Alphabet’s search and ads.

If customers slow AI adoption, cut cloud spending or hold back on TPU style systems, Alphabet’s cloud related revenue and group earnings could disappoint. IVW still carries that risk through its 9.08% stake in Alphabet, but its positions in sectors such as pharmaceuticals and retail tie more of the outcome to healthcare demand and consumer spending patterns instead of a single company’s AI and cloud story.

Ten companies make up 58.9% of IVW. Find out which ones, and how much each carries.

Choosing your Alphabet exposure through funds

If you want Alphabet in size without stock picking, IWF and IVW sit closest together. Each US$1,000 puts roughly US$100 or US$91 into Alphabet and both charge US$18 a year on a US$10,000 holding. The real split is what surrounds it. IWF leans harder into semiconductors and hardware, while IVW spreads more into pharmaceuticals and multi sector holdings.

VUG asks a different question. It holds fewer companies than IWF and IVW, charges about US$3 a year on US$10,000 and tilts more toward its biggest positions. That can matter if a cyber incident like the recent Air Force cloud breach changes how investors view large tech platforms. Your first decision is simple. Do you want the extra concentration, or would you rather pay more to spread Alphabet’s cloud and advertising risks, including its high level of non cash earnings, across more holdings?

data.description:

That is the question many investors are asking now that copper and gold prices are recovering and oil is still firm, while zinc has reacted to smelter cuts and higher energy costs. Global X Copper Miners ETF (COPX)

Holdings: 47 | In metals and mining: 99.3% of the fund

This ETF gathers copper focused miners, with a heavy tilt to diversified metals companies. BHP Group at 5.45%, Boliden at 5.41% and Anglo American at 5.14% give you large producers whose revenue is tied to copper, while BHP and Anglo American also have meaningful iron ore and other metals output. Recovering copper prices can lift the value of ore sold for all three, and the small 3.0% gold sleeve means gold’s rebound touches the portfolio but does not steer it.

Investors are also leaning on Simply Wall St’s view that about 61.6% of COPX by weight sits in holdings trading below fair value. That upside case competes with real risks if copper, gold or zinc prices soften again or if energy and labour costs erode margins at miners. BHP and Boliden together come to 10.9% of the fund, so BHP only carries slightly more weight than Boliden.

See how COPX's price compares with analysts' targets for its holdings.

Global X Silver Miners ETF (SIL)

Holdings: 43 | In metals and mining: 99.8% of the fund

This ETF tilts heavily to gold and silver miners, with Wheaton Precious Metals at 25.11% and Pan American Silver at 10.79% together making up 35.9% of the fund. Recovering gold prices feed directly into potential revenue for Wheaton, while Pan American Silver and Coeur Mining at 9.28% connect you to silver production and some by product exposure to other metals. That mix gives you a focused way to look at precious metal miners rather than the broader blend you get in COPX.

Simply Wall St estimates that about 81% of this ETF by weight is in holdings trading below fair value, which may be a reason for investors to explore it further. You are still heavily reliant on the direction of gold and silver prices and on mining costs staying under control, so the concentration in a few large holdings gives you clear exposure but leaves plenty of uncertainty.

Global X Lithium & Battery Tech ETF (LIT)

Holdings: 45 | In metals and mining: 30.4% of the fund

RIO is the anchor here as a large diversified miner with meaningful copper exposure, while Albemarle and NAURA Technology Group tilt you toward lithium chemicals and equipment tied to chip and electronics manufacturing. Those three together come to 24.9% of LIT, which gives you a mix of miners, specialty chemicals and hardware suppliers that react differently when metal prices move. Recovering copper prices speak most directly to RIO’s sales, while Albemarle and NAURA connect you to the demand side through batteries and semiconductor gear rather than just raw ore.

Most of this ETF’s money sits outside metals and mining in areas such as electrical components, specialty chemicals and car manufacturers. As a result, you are partly betting on the wider battery and electronics chain rather than only on miners reacting to copper, gold or zinc prices. Simply Wall St’s estimate that 49.1% of holdings by weight trade below fair value gives investors one more angle to research. However, you are still depending on a relatively small 30.4% metals slice to carry the direct commodity story.

What separates these funds

If you want your money tightly tied to miners that could feel recovering copper, gold and zinc prices most directly, COPX and SIL are the closer pair. COPX leans on diversified and copper focused miners and has 99.3% in metals and mining, with its top positions spread fairly evenly. LIT is different. Only 30.4% is in diversified miners and the rest runs through electrical equipment, chemicals and car makers tied to the battery chain. That mix means miners such as Rio Tinto link you to copper, while businesses like Tesla and Albemarle lean more on battery demand than on spot metal prices. If energy costs rise faster than copper, gold and zinc prices, any benefit to miners inside these funds can shrink. The real choice rests with you and the type of investor you are, whether you want concentrated precious metals exposure with SIL, broader copper focused miners with COPX, or LIT’s more mixed battery and metals story. Readers hoping to buy Texas Pacific Land Corporation (NYSE:TPL) for its dividend will need to make their move shortly, as the stock is about to trade ex-dividend. The ex-dividend date is one business day before the record date, which is the cut-off date for shareholders to be present on the company's books to be eligible for a dividend payment. It is important to be aware of the ex-dividend date because any trade on the stock needs to have been settled on or before the record date. Therefore, if you purchase Texas Pacific Land's shares on or after the 1st of December, you won't be eligible to receive the dividend, when it is paid on the 15th of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$0.60 per share, on the back of last year when the company paid a total of US$2.40 to shareholders. Based on the last year's worth of payments, Texas Pacific Land has a trailing yield of 0.9% on the current stock price of US$261.37. We love seeing companies pay a dividend, but it's also important to be sure that laying the golden eggs isn't going to kill our golden goose! As a result, readers should always check whether Texas Pacific Land has been able to grow its dividends, or if the dividend might be cut.

Dividends are typically paid out of company income, so if a company pays out more than it earned, its dividend is usually at a higher risk of being cut. Fortunately Texas Pacific Land's payout ratio is modest, at just 27% of profit. Yet cash flow is typically more important than profit for assessing dividend sustainability, so we should always check if the company generated enough cash to afford its dividend. Over the past year it paid out 136% of its free cash flow as dividends, which is uncomfortably high. It's hard to consistently pay out more cash than you generate without either borrowing or using company cash, so we'd wonder how the company justifies this payout level.

Texas Pacific Land paid out less in dividends than it reported in profits, but unfortunately it didn't generate enough cash to cover the dividend. Were this to happen repeatedly, this would be a risk to Texas Pacific Land's ability to maintain its dividend.

Stocks in companies that generate sustainable earnings growth often make the best dividend prospects, as it is easier to lift the dividend when earnings are rising. It's encouraging to see Texas Pacific Land has grown its earnings rapidly, up 28% a year for the past five years.
